name: Affirming a disjunct
statement: Affirming a disjunct runs from 'A or B' and A to not-B, and how often people draw it tracks whether the content makes the two clauses incompatible.
meaning: The form has two premises and a conclusion. The first premise says A or B. The second asserts A. The conclusion asserts not-B. Read inclusively, 'A or B' is true when both hold, so nothing rules B out and the step fails. Read exclusively, as 'A or B but not both', the step is valid and there is no fallacy to name. That is the whole of the dispute, and it makes the interesting question an empirical one about how a disjunction is understood rather than a formal one about how it is written. The valid neighbour is the disjunctive syllogism, which asserts not-A and concludes B, and which is drawn readily. Two other named fallacies sit close by and are different arguments. Affirming the consequent asserts q from 'if p then q' and q. Denying the antecedent asserts not-q from 'if p then q' and not-p. Those two share an experimental apparatus, the four conditional inference forms put to the same participants, and the Atlas entries on them carry the figures, which are not restated here. The Atlas also covers false dilemma, where the major premise states an incompatibility rather than a disjunction and the invalid steps are the denials. The experimental work on this form is thin by comparison with any of them, and what exists measures two things separately: how people read a disjunction, and what they conclude when a categorical premise is added to it.

origin.who: Ana Cristina Quelhas and P. N. Johnson-Laird
origin.note: The name belongs to logic and no priority is claimed for this paper. Brian Kirby was arguing about the fallacy under this name in Informal Logic in 1986, and quotes Monroe Beardsley's textbook Thinking Straight and Irving Copi's Introduction to Logic as the sources that teach it. This paper is placed here because it is the study read for this entry that put the inference itself to participants and counted the answers. Earlier experimental work on disjunctive reasoning exists and could not be read: Evans and Newstead in Psychological Research in 1980, and Newstead, Griggs and Chrostowski in the Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology in 1984, are both closed at their publishers. The article appeared online in March 2016 and in the 2017 volume.

evidence: Quelhas and Johnson-Laird ran three experiments in Lisbon, in Portuguese, on students at ISPA. The first asked 44 of them to list the situations a disjunction leaves possible, six contents for each of four sorts of disjunction, 24 trials in all. Nine were dropped for treating both clauses being false as possible on more than half the problems, leaving 35. For a plain disjunction with nothing in the content pushing either way, 24 of the 35 gave the exclusive pattern as their predominant answer and 7 gave the inclusive pattern, with four miscellaneous. No participant gave the inclusive pattern for a disjunction whose content rules out both clauses holding together, Fisher-Yates exact test p < .01, one-tailed. Fit to the predicted interpretations ranked exclusive disjunctions at 3.7, the two content-modulated sorts at 2.3 each and plain disjunctions at 1.6, Kendall's W = .49, chi-square(3) = 51.8. The second experiment gave 88 students, 70 women and 18 men of average age 19, 48 problems pairing a disjunction with a categorical premise, and three answers to choose between. Given a plain disjunction and the premise A, 54% chose that B may or may not hold, which is what an inclusive reading licenses. Given a disjunction whose content makes the clauses incompatible, 96% drew not-B. Given one whose content makes the second clause follow from the first, as in 'Andre is in Lisbon or he is in Portugal', 74% drew B. Across all 16 problem types 64% of evaluations matched the theory's predictions against a chance rate of one in three, Wilcoxon z = 8.153. Looking at each participant's predominant answers to plain disjunctions, 24% treated the disjunction as exclusive or came within one answer of it, 19% held that nothing follows from an affirmative categorical, and 22% gave that answer to all four categoricals. The third experiment asked 80 students to write their own conclusions rather than pick one, 36 trials each, with two judges coding the answers at Cohen's kappa = .96. Plain disjunctions were dropped from it. Given the premise A, the conclusion not-B was written by 80% where the content excludes both clauses holding, by 44% where the content leaves the second clause open, and by 32% where the content makes the second clause follow. In the second and third of those the conclusion is wrong, and the right answers, that nothing follows and that B holds, were given by 32% and 45%. The predicted rank order across the three sorts held, Page's L = 1068.0, z = 8.5, p < .0000003. Nicolae, Petrenco, Tsilia and Marty measured the reading rather than the inference, and at a scale nothing else here approaches. They recruited 564 people on Prolific, native speakers of English (90), French (127), Romanian (111), Russian (107) and Greek (129), and showed each a story in three scenes: a situation, a character guessing that one of two things will happen, and an outcome in which both happen. Rejecting the guess counts as an exclusive reading. Responses from 37 people, 6.5% of the sample, were dropped for missing a threshold of 80% accuracy on control trials that was set in advance. Rejection rates for the simple disjunction, 'A or B' in English, ran from 20% in Romanian to 54% in Greek. For the complex forms, 'either A or B' in English and reiterated particles in the other four languages, eight of the nine language-by-form cells fell between 60% and 75%. About 80% of participants answered the same way on all three target items, from 73% in Greek to 82% in English and Romanian. Among all participants, consistent inclusive responders were 54% for the simple disjunction, 30% and 20% for the two complex ones, and consistent exclusive responders were 25%, 48% and 63%. The hypotheses and analysis plan for the English experiment were registered on AsPredicted through the Open Science Framework in December 2020, before data collection, and the data are posted there.

replication.headline: The inference has been measured directly in one laboratory, in one paper, in Portuguese. A search for any independent repetition of that measurement found none.
replication.detail: Quelhas and Johnson-Laird's second and third experiments repeat the finding on separate samples of 88 and 80 with different response formats, choosing among three conclusions and then writing one's own, and the same content dependence appears in both. That is one laboratory repeating itself inside one paper, which is why the state here is none-located rather than replicated. Searches for an independent repetition covered Crossref, Semantic Scholar, Unpaywall, Europe PMC and open-web search, under the fallacy's name and under the schema, and turned up nothing that puts 'A or B' with the premise A to participants and counts the conclusions. The interpretive half of the claim does have independent large-sample support pointing partly the other way. Nicolae and colleagues tested 564 people across five languages with a preregistered English experiment and found that no disjunction they tested is read exclusively by everyone, that simple disjunctions draw exclusive readings at rates as low as 20%, and that consistent inclusive responders outnumbered exclusive ones for the simple disjunction by 54% to 25%. Quelhas and Johnson-Laird's plain Portuguese disjunctions, by contrast, drew a predominantly exclusive reading from 24 of 35 participants, and their own note says the plain items named two different people, which they raise as a possible reason. The two results are not a replication pair, since the tasks and the materials differ, and they are the reason this page treats the exclusive reading as a property of the wording and the content rather than of reasoners.

limits: There is no standardised effect size on this page. The studies report percentages, rank orders and non-parametric tests, and Quelhas and Johnson-Laird say they used distribution-free tests throughout. The samples are students at one institution in Lisbon, and the materials are Portuguese, so the reading of a Portuguese 'ou' carries the result. Nicolae and colleagues show that the marker matters: within a single language the simple and the complex form of the disjunction drew different rates, and across languages the simple forms varied by more than thirty points. Their English figure for the simple disjunction is plotted in their Figure 2, and the running text of their results gives only the cross-language range, so no English rate is quoted above. The 54% in the second Quelhas experiment is the rate of the correct answer, not the rate of the fallacy. Its Table 2 prints only the predicted response and its percentage for each of the 16 cells, so the split of the remaining answers between B and not-B is not recoverable from the table, and nothing here should be read as a count of participants who affirmed the disjunct on plain disjunctions. The rates of 44% and 32% in the third experiment are counts of that conclusion, and both come from disjunctions whose content is doing work. That experiment also carries a headcount that does not agree with itself: its method says eighty students took part, and its results say the analysis rests on 80 participants after two were excluded for failing the practice problems. Several papers that bear on the reading of 'or' were searched for and not obtained. Evans and Newstead's 1980 study of disjunctive reasoning, Newstead, Griggs and Chrostowski's 1984 study with realistic disjunctives, Braine and Rumain's 1981 developmental study of 'or', and Chevallier and colleagues' 2008 study of exclusive readings are all closed at their publishers, with Unpaywall recording no open copy. Jasbi and Frank's 2021 paper in Collabra is open access, and the publisher's bot check refused the file on repeated attempts. Nothing from any of them is reported here.
misreadings: The commonest error is to confuse the fallacy with the valid form beside it. The disjunctive syllogism asserts not-A and concludes B, and it is one of the easiest inferences there is. Affirming a disjunct asserts A and concludes not-B. Reversing the sign of the second premise is the whole difference between an inference and a mistake. The second error is to file it with the two conditional fallacies. Affirming the consequent runs from 'if p then q' and q to p, denying the antecedent runs from 'if p then q' and not-p to not-q, and the Atlas keeps all three apart because the experiments do. The third error is to treat the word 'fallacy' as closing the question, and this is the case where that reading is least safe. Kirby's article in Informal Logic argues that ordinary 'or' is often strong, gives a threat as his example and a rebuttal between two naturalists as another, and holds that where the disjunction is strong the manoeuvre is valid. He also disputes the textbook advice, which he quotes from Richard Jeffrey, that an 'or' should be taken inclusively in the absence of indications to the contrary. His target is teaching, and his claim is that presenting the form as a formal fallacy misleads students. The fourth error is to reach for the illusory-inference literature, which is about a different schema and reports much higher rates. Johnson-Laird and Savary's illusions are built from a disjunction of two conditionals, as in 'if king then ace, or else if not king then ace' followed by 'there is a king', and their 16 Princeton participants drew the predicted invalid conclusion on 100% of both illusions while rating their confidence at 4.4 on a five-point scale. Their control problems, which are closer to the form on this page, were answered correctly at 88% and 100%. Khemlani and Johnson-Laird's later work moves to embedded disjunctions of the shape 'A or else (B or else C)'. Neither programme is measuring 'A or B' with the premise A, and quoting a rate from one for the other is the mistake this page exists to prevent. The last error is to read any of these rates as a fact about people. The same participants who drew not-B from 80% of one sort of disjunction drew it from 32% of another, and the difference was the content of the clauses.

sources.text: Quelhas, A. C., & Johnson-Laird, P. N. (2017). The modulation of disjunctive assertions. Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology, 70(4), 703-717. Read in full as the PDF hosted at modeltheory.org, downloaded twice from two different paths with the tables re-extracted each time. Source for the three experiments, the samples of 44, 88 and 80, and every percentage, rank order and test statistic attributed to them.

Nicolae, A. C., Petrenco, A., Tsilia, A., & Marty, P. (2024). Do Languages Have Exclusive Disjunctions? Open Mind, 8, 1469-1485. Read as the JATS XML from Europe PMC, PMC11666282, downloaded twice with identical checksums. Source for the 564 participants, the exclusions, the rejection rates by language and disjunction type, the responder proportions and the preregistration.

Johnson-Laird, P. N., & Savary, F. (1999). Illusory inferences: a novel class of erroneous deductions. Cognition, 71(3), 191-229. Read in full as a PDF, with Table 4 and the confidence ratings extracted twice. Source for the illusion and control problems of Experiment 1, the 16 participants, the 100% figures and the 88% control.

Khemlani, S., & Johnson-Laird, P. N. (2009). Disjunctive illusory inferences and how to eliminate them. Memory & Cognition, 37(5), 615-623. Read as the PDF at Springer. Cited only for the embedded-disjunction schema its abstract and introduction describe.

Kirby, B. (1986). A Plea For Affirming a Disjunct. Informal Logic, 8(3). Read in full as the open-access PDF. Source for the argument that ordinary 'or' is often strong, the quotation of Jeffrey's advice on the default reading, and the attribution of the teaching of the fallacy to Beardsley and Copi.

Evans, J. St. B. T., & Newstead, S. E. (1980). A study of disjunctive reasoning. Psychological Research, 41(4), 373-388. Closed at the publisher, and Unpaywall returns no open location. Named here because it was searched for and not obtained.

Newstead, S. E., Griggs, R. A., & Chrostowski, J. J. (1984). Reasoning with Realistic Disjunctives. The Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology Section A, 36(4), 611-627. Closed at the publisher, and Unpaywall returns no open location. Named here because it was searched for and not obtained.

Braine, M. D. S., & Rumain, B. (1981). Development of comprehension of "or": Evidence for a sequence of competencies. Journal of Experimental Child Psychology, 31(1), 46-70. Closed at the publisher, and Unpaywall returns no open location. Named here because it was searched for and not obtained, and nothing is reported from it.

Chevallier, C., Noveck, I. A., Nazir, T., Bott, L., Lanzetti, V., & Sperber, D. (2008). Making disjunctions exclusive. Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology, 61(11), 1741-1760. Closed at the publisher, and Unpaywall returns no open location. Named here because it was searched for and not obtained.
